current_leader.name: Corporate promised-refund settlement watchdog
current_leader.state_transition: vendor or merchant promises a refund or credit -> expected receivable is created from email/ERP/card context -> card or bank credit does not arrive, arrives short, or arrives after expected window -> system detects mismatch before dispute/escalation deadline -> prepares or sends evidence-based recovery action -> recovered amount is measured
current_leader.why_survived: The event exists naturally in email, ERP, card and bank data; the intervention can be read-only until escalation; the financial delta is exact; performance pricing maps naturally to recovered money; consumer/single-merchant tools prove the pattern, while this run did not find a dominant cross-vendor B2B product whose narrow job is to convert refund promises into expected receivables, verify settlement across corporate accounts, and automatically escalate missing/short credits before issuer deadlines.
strongest_evidence: RefundIQ demonstrates automated matching of refund promises/communications against bank activity and escalation when refunds are missing, validating the event pattern in consumer finance.
Recoup Hero demonstrates bank matching and dispute-draft generation for missing refunds in a single-merchant context.
Enterprise reconciliation products such as Cointab and Phacet explicitly identify missing or mismatched refunds, proving the data can be reconciled at scale but also creating competitive pressure.
Corporate-card dispute processes commonly provide finite windows around 120 days and require supporting evidence, creating an external deadline for intervention.
current_leader.closest_threat: Broad enterprise reconciliation and spend-management platforms can already identify refund mismatches and could absorb promise-to-settlement tracking as a feature. The actual enterprise dollar pool of vendor-promised refunds that never or incorrectly settle is not yet quantified.
current_leader.smallest_intervention: Read authorized email/ERP/accounting/card/bank feeds; extract each vendor refund promise into an expected-refund receivable with amount, date and reference; match incoming credits including partial credits; flag overdue or short settlement; generate an evidence packet and escalation/dispute draft. Do not move money or sit on the payment path.
current_leader.monetization: Small percentage of objectively recovered missing/short refunds or a fixed fee per successfully recovered refund. Performance pricing is stronger here than for app-wide configuration optimization because each recovered receivable is individually attributable.
current_leader.biggest_unresolved_risk: Need evidence that missing or short corporate refunds are frequent and large enough outside ecommerce/platform-specific reconciliation, and that broad reconciliation/expense suites do not already neutralize the narrow promise-to-settlement workflow.
current_leader.next_research_test: Quantify enterprise vendor-refund leakage and search exact B2B software for expected-refund receivables: systems that ingest refund promises or credit memos, match them to corporate card/bank credits, track issuer/vendor deadlines, and recover missing/short refunds on a performance basis. Kill if broad spend/reconciliation incumbents already do this end-to-end or if leakage is economically trivial.

rejections.reason: Exact automation/performance-priced incumbents already identify unused labels and automatically obtain refunds or void labels.
Current healthcare authorization systems already track expiration and explicitly flag authorizations that expire before scheduled service.

runner_ups.reason: Excellent quota/reset trigger and measurable overage avoidance, but still lacks one proven high-value vertical with large recurring leakage and easy non-proxy scheduling.

Apple recovery-by-day data proves a real cost/recovery tradeoff for high-variable-cost apps, but the setting is app-wide, infrequently changed, easy to approximate with a spreadsheet, and hard to attribute for performance pricing.
Real prepaid expiry exists, but mature routing platforms can absorb expiry-aware allocation.

new_search_rules: A financially non-trivial configuration choice is still a weak tollbooth if it changes only occasionally; favor repeated unit-level events with per-event attribution.

Cross-system promised-value versus actual-settlement events are attractive because an unstructured promise can be converted into a machine-readable receivable and matched to an objective cash/card event.
When exact recovery automation already exists in one narrow vertical, do not generalize the wedge without proving a different cross-system or cross-vendor mechanism and whitespace.
Finite dispute or claim deadlines strengthen intervention value only when the upstream expected-value event is independently machine-readable.

evidence.finding: Apple reports roughly 40% of successful recoveries within 3 days, 75% within 16 days, and 90% within 28 days, showing the grace-duration decision can be economically modeled.
Apple supports 3, 16 and 28 day grace periods and provider-native recovery.
Unused unscanned shipping labels can be programmatically refunded within carrier windows.
Existing automation monitors unused UPS labels and shares recovered refunds, neutralizing the obvious wedge.
Upcoming payer APIs expose prior-authorization approval and end-date/circumstance, making expiration machine-readable.
Enterprise reconciliation software already identifies refund mismatches, proving scale but creating adjacent competition.
